zalmaqum.t: Zalmaqum, a league of small kingdoms around Harran in the Balikh valley, known from the Mari letters of the 18th century BCE.
zalmaqum.o: Zalmaqum was the name of a region of northern Mesopotamia around Harran and the upper Balikh river. In the 18th century BCE its four kings acted together as a loose confederacy, alongside the Amorite tribal groups who moved seasonally through the steppe.
zalmaqum.r: The Mari archives record that the kings of Zalmaqum and Yaminite tribal leaders swore an alliance in the temple of the moon god Sin at Harran, already an important sanctuary. They negotiated with Mari, Yamhad and the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, but no texts from the confederacy itself survive.
zalmaqum.e: The confederacy disappears from the record after the fall of Mari c. 1760 BCE. Harran remained a major city and centre of the moon cult into the Islamic period.

zeta-under-the-crnojevici.t: Last free Serbian Orthodox principality of the 15th-century Balkans, where Ivan Crnojević founded Cetinje and his son set up the first South Slav printing press.
zeta-under-the-crnojevici.o: After the decline of the Balšić lords and the Serbian Despotate, the Crnojević family took the lead in the mountains of Zeta. Stefan Crnojević, ruling from around 1451, allied with Venice and joined Skanderbeg's League of Lezhë, holding the territory around Lake Skadar and the highlands behind the Bay of Kotor.
zeta-under-the-crnojevici.r: The principality was a confederation of mountain clans led by a hereditary lord who balanced Venetian alliance against Ottoman pressure. Ivan Crnojević moved his seat from Žabljak to Cetinje in 1482 and founded a monastery there in 1484. His son Đurađ opened a printing press that produced the Oktoih in 1494, among the first Cyrillic books printed.
zeta-under-the-crnojevici.e: Ottoman pressure forced Đurađ Crnojević to flee to Venice in 1496, and Zeta was absorbed into the Ottoman sanjak of Scutari. Leadership of the highlands passed to the metropolitans of Cetinje, laying the ground for the Prince-Bishopric of Montenegro.

zurayid-dynasty.t: An Isma'ili dynasty that ruled the port of Aden and grew rich on Indian Ocean trade between the Sulayhid and Ayyubid eras.
zurayid-dynasty.o: The Banu Zuray, a branch of the Yam tribe of Hamdan, were appointed governors of Aden by the Sulayhid dynasty around 1083, when the brothers al-Abbas and al-Mas'ud ibn Karam shared the city. As Sulayhid power faded under Queen Arwa they became independent rulers.
zurayid-dynasty.r: The Zurayids profited from Aden's role as the main port between Egypt and India; the documents of the Cairo Geniza describe Jewish and Muslim merchants trading pepper, textiles and metals through the harbour. They followed the Hafizi branch of Isma'ilism, recognised by the Fatimid court in Cairo. Saba ibn Abi al-Su'ud consolidated their rule in the 1130s and they extended inland to Ta'izz and Dhu Jibla.
zurayid-dynasty.e: In 1174 the Ayyubid prince Turan-Shah invaded Yemen and took Aden, ending the dynasty. Aden remained Yemen's chief port under Ayyubid Yemen and the Rasulid dynasty.

zacazgo-of-hunza.t: The northern Muisca realm of the zaque, ruled from Hunza, the site of modern Tunja, and long the rival of the zipa of Bacatá.
zacazgo-of-hunza.o: Hunza, now Tunja in Boyacá, became the seat of the zaque, ruler of the northern Muisca territories, in the centuries before the Spanish conquest. Muisca tradition named Hunzahúa as its first ruler and claimed the zaques descended from him.
zacazgo-of-hunza.r: The zaque ruled through lesser chiefs and received tribute in gold, cloth and goods. Succession passed from a ruler to his sister's son. Hunza was a centre of trade in salt, emeralds, cotton and gold. The zaques fought repeated wars with the zipas of the Zipazgo of Bacatá, including a battle in which the zipa Saguamanchica and the zaque Michuá were both killed around 1490.
zacazgo-of-hunza.e: In 1537 Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada seized Hunza and captured the aged zaque Quemuenchatocha. His successor Aquiminzaque was executed in 1540. The Spanish founded Tunja on the site in 1539, and it became a major town of the New Kingdom of Granada.

zenu.t: Chiefdoms of Colombia's Caribbean lowlands that built a vast network of drained fields and canals and produced some of the finest goldwork of pre-Columbian America.
zenu.o: The Zenú, or Sinú, lived in the floodplains of the Sinú and San Jorge rivers and the Mojana depression in northern Colombia. From around 200 BCE they began building an extensive system of parallel canals and raised ridges to control seasonal flooding, eventually covering hundreds of thousands of hectares.
zenu.r: Spanish accounts describe three linked provinces, Finzenú, Panzenú and Zenufana, each ruled by a chief. The hydraulic works supported dense farming of maize and cassava, as well as fishing. The Zenú were skilled goldsmiths, casting filigree earrings and figurines, and their burial mounds held rich gold offerings. They also wove fibre from cane flecha, a skill that survives in the modern sombrero vueltiao.
zenu.e: The canal system had largely gone out of use by about 1000 CE, but Zenú society persisted. Spaniards from Cartagena looted their tombs from 1534, and colonial rule, disease and forced labour broke up the chiefdoms. Zenú descendants live today in the reserve of San Andrés de Sotavento.

zalpa.t: Zalpa, a city-state on the Black Sea coast that rivalled Nesa and figures in the oldest Hittite legend, the tale of the queen of Kanesh's thirty sons.
zalpa.o: Zalpuwa lay on the Black Sea near the mouth of the Kızılırmak river. In the early 2nd millennium BCE it was one of the native Anatolian kingdoms competing for power with Kanesh, and the Hittites remembered it in a legend of thirty sons of the queen of Kanesh who drifted there in baskets.
zalpa.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. The Anitta text records that Uhna, king of Zalpuwa, carried off the statue of the god of Nesa, and that Anitta later captured Huzziya of Zalpuwa and brought the statue home.
zalpa.e: Zalpa resisted the early Hittite kings for years. According to the Hittite Zalpa text, it was besieged and finally destroyed in the time of Hattusili I, c. 1650 BCE, and its land became part of the Hittite Empire.

zipazgo-of-bacata.t: The southern Muisca realm of the zipa, centred on the savanna of Bogotá, the most powerful native state in Colombia when the Spanish arrived.
zipazgo-of-bacata.o: Bacatá, on the high savanna where Bogotá now stands, became the seat of the zipa, ruler of the southern Muisca, in the 15th century. Muisca tradition names Meicuchuca as an early zipa, and Saguamanchica expanded the realm by conquering neighbouring chiefdoms such as Fusagasugá.
zipazgo-of-bacata.r: The zipa ruled through subordinate chiefs who paid tribute and supplied warriors. Succession went from uncle to nephew, and heirs were trained in seclusion. Nemequene, who reigned in the early 16th century, is credited with a code of laws. The realm controlled the salt mines of Zipaquirá and Nemocón, whose salt was traded widely. Lake Guatavita, a sacred lake, lay within its territory. Wars with the zaque of the Zacazgo of Hunza were frequent.
zipazgo-of-bacata.e: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada entered the savanna in 1537. The zipa Tisquesusa died fighting that year, and his successor Sagipa died in Spanish captivity in 1539 after being tortured for gold. Santa Fe de Bogotá was founded in 1538 as capital of the New Kingdom of Granada.

zachlumia.t: Medieval principality of Hum in Herzegovina and southern Dalmatia, home of the Miroslav Gospel and contested by Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia.
zachlumia.o: Hum emerged among Slavs settled between the Neretva and Dubrovnik in the 7th to 9th centuries. Its best-known early ruler, Mihajlo Višević, governed in the early 10th century, allied with Simeon I of the First Bulgarian Empire and attending church councils at Split.
zachlumia.r: Princes ruled from Ston and Bona near Blagaj, over a population divided between Catholic and Orthodox churches. Hum often fell under neighbours: Duklja, the Kingdom of Croatia and later the Grand Principality of Serbia. Prince Miroslav, brother of Stefan Nemanja, ruled it in the late 12th century and commissioned the Miroslav Gospel, a masterpiece of Cyrillic illumination.
zachlumia.e: In 1326 Stephen II Kotromanić of the Banate of Bosnia took most of Hum, and in 1333 Ston and Pelješac were sold to the Republic of Ragusa. The region later became the core of Herzegovina.

zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.t: The Zaydi Shi'a imamate founded at Sa'dah in 897, a religious state in the northern Yemeni highlands that lasted, in various forms, until 1962.
zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.o: In 897 Yahya ibn al-Husayn, a descendant of al-Hasan from the Hejaz, came to Sa'dah at the invitation of feuding tribes. As Imam al-Hadi ila al-Haqq he settled their disputes and founded a Zaydi state, establishing the doctrine that any learned descendant of Ali and Fatima who claimed the imamate by rising against injustice could be imam.
zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.r: The imamate had no hereditary succession; rival claimants often contested it, and its reach rarely extended far beyond the northern highlands and Sa'dah. Imams depended on the support of tribes such as Hashid and Bakil. al-Mansur Abd Allah ibn Hamza in the 13th century revived its strength against the Ayyubids, and it competed with the Sulayhids, Rasulids and Tahirids.
zaydi-imamate-of-yemen.e: Imam Sharaf al-Din Yahya expanded the state in the early 16th century, but the Ottoman Empire conquered most of Yemen after 1538. In 1597 al-Qasim ibn Muhammad proclaimed himself imam and began the revolt that created the Qasimid State.

zancle.t: Greek city on the Strait of Messina, named after its sickle-shaped harbour and renamed Messana in the 5th century BCE, which controlled the passage between Sicily and Italy.
zancle.o: Settlers from Cumae and Chalcis founded Zancle in the second half of the 8th century BCE, at first as a base of 'pirates', on the sickle-shaped peninsula that gave the city its name (zanklon, sickle). Facing Rhegion across the Strait, it commanded one of the most important sea passages of the Mediterranean.
zancle.r: Zancle founded Mylae and Himera and grew rich on traffic through the Strait. Around 490 BCE refugees from Samos seized it, and soon afterwards Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegion, took it, settled Messenians from the Peloponnese and renamed it Messana. It was later a democracy, sided at times with Athens, and was destroyed by the Carthaginian general Himilco in 396 BCE before Dionysius I refounded it.
zancle.e: In 288 BCE Campanian mercenaries, the Mamertines, seized Messana and killed or expelled many citizens. Their appeal to Rome in 264 BCE triggered the First Punic War. The city became Roman Messana and is today Messina.

zeta-under-the-balsici.t: Principality of the Balšić family on the shores of Lake Skadar and the Adriatic, a successor of the Serbian Empire contested with Venice and the Ottomans.
zeta-under-the-balsici.o: Around 1356, after Stefan Dušan's death, Balša I and his sons Stracimir, Đurađ I and Balša II took control of Zeta, the land around Lake Skadar and the Gulf of Kotor, ruling from Skadar (Shkodër).
zeta-under-the-balsici.r: The Balšići ruled as lords of Zeta with nobles and coastal towns, fighting Ragusa, Bosnia and Albanian lords. Balša II took Valona and Durrës, but died fighting the Ottomans at Savra in 1385. His successor Đurađ II Stracimirović gave Skadar to Venice in 1396 to escape Ottoman pressure. Balša III fought long wars with Venice over Skadar and the coast.
zeta-under-the-balsici.e: Balša III died in 1421, leaving Zeta to his uncle, Despot Stefan Lazarević of Serbia. Venice kept the coastal towns, and the inland region later became the Principality of Zeta under the Crnojević family.

zaporozhian-sich.t: The fortified island camp of the Zaporozhian Cossacks below the Dnieper rapids, a self-governing warrior republic and symbol of Ukrainian freedom.
zaporozhian-sich.o: From the 15th century runaway peasants, adventurers and townsmen gathered on the steppe frontier as Cossacks, fishing, hunting and fighting the Tatars. Around 1552 Prince Dmytro Vyshnevetsky built a fort on the island of Mala Khortytsia, often seen as the first Sich. Later Siches were built at several sites beyond the rapids, out of reach of royal officials.
zaporozhian-sich.r: The Sich was a male military community governed by a general assembly, the rada, which elected the kish otaman and other officers. Cossacks were Orthodox and lived in barracks by units called kurins. They raided Ottoman and Crimean coasts in light boats, served the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for pay and often rebelled against it. Bohdan Khmelnytsky's uprising began there in 1648.
zaporozhian-sich.e: Peter I destroyed the Sich in 1709 because its Cossacks joined Mazepa. A new Sich was allowed in 1734, but in 1775 Catherine II's army surrounded and abolished it, exiling the last otaman Petro Kalnyshevsky. Its Cossacks dispersed to the Danube Sich and later the Black Sea Cossack Host.

ziyadid-dynasty.t: The first Islamic dynasty of Yemen's coastal plain, which founded Zabid as its capital and ruled the Tihama for two centuries.
ziyadid-dynasty.o: In 818 or 819 the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun sent Muhammad ibn Ziyad, a descendant of the Umayyad governor Ziyad ibn Abihi, to subdue rebellious tribes in the Tihama. He founded the city of Zabid as his base and established a hereditary emirate, recognising Abbasid sovereignty.
ziyadid-dynasty.r: The Ziyadids ruled the Red Sea coastal plain and at times claimed authority over Hadramawt and the highlands. Zabid became a walled city and a leading centre of Sunni learning. Real power often lay with Ethiopian slave ministers; Husayn ibn Salamah, regent in the late 10th century, built mosques and roads linking Zabid with Mecca and Hadramawt.
ziyadid-dynasty.e: In the early 11th century the last Ziyadid was a child under the control of slave commanders. Around 1018 one of them, Najah, took power, founding the Najahid dynasty. Zabid's mosques and scholarly tradition survived and made it a UNESCO World Heritage city.

zengid-dynasty.t: The Turkish dynasty of Zengi and Nur al-Din that united Muslim Syria against the Crusaders and prepared the way for Saladin.
zengid-dynasty.o: Imad al-Din Zengi, son of a Seljuk governor, was appointed atabeg of Mosul in 1127 and took Aleppo in 1128. In 1144 he captured Edessa, destroying the County of Edessa's capital, before being murdered in 1146.
zengid-dynasty.r: His son Nur al-Din ruled from Aleppo, took Damascus in 1154 and united Syria. He promoted Sunni revival with madrasas, the Nuri hospital in Damascus, and a court for complaints, and presented his wars as jihad. He sent Shirkuh and Saladin to Egypt, where Saladin became vizier in 1169. Other Zengids ruled Mosul, Sinjar and Jazirat ibn Umar as Turkish atabegs of a largely Arab and Kurdish population.
zengid-dynasty.e: After Nur al-Din died in 1174, Saladin took over Syria and reduced the Zengid branches to vassals. The Mosul line lasted until Badr al-Din Lu'lu' displaced it in the 1230s, and minor branches survived until about 1250.
